TL;DR: `buf_write()` → BufWriteCmd → Lua `M.save()` → `nvim__term_capture()` → C ansi export

## Problem:
Terminal buffer content and metadata are lost once the terminal
process exits.

## Solution:
- Register a `TermOpen` autocmd in the `nvim.terminal` augroup
  that creates a per-buffer `BufWriteCmd` handler for each
  terminal buffer. The write path is driven by Lua, calling into C
  only for ANSI export (`termgetansi()`).

- `:write` without args: derive a filename from the terminal URI
  and save to `stdpath('state')/term/<name>.mpack`.

- `:write {name}`: save to the user-specified path.

- Range writes (like `:'<,'>w`, `:1,5w`) export the selected line
  range as ANSI.

## For future enhancement:
~~- cwd unreliable. Now cwd is the job's cwd at spawn time, parsed from the `term://` buffer URI.~~
- [if someone requests] Alternate screen cannot be saved.

## NOTE:
~~- PID is preserved in the URI-derived filename to avoid collisions.~~
- `:write >>` is explicitly rejected (E5008).
- Alternate screen rejects `:write`.

ref https://github.com/neovim/neovim/issues/40017

comment_data.body: this is fine as a temporary approach but let's plan to revisit later, see https://github.com/neovim/neovim/issues/40017#issuecomment-4623175666

saving as a string isn't great, it loses information (quoting rules are nasty, and `shell_argv_to_str` doesn't really even attempt to handle complex quoting...)

this makes me think it would be worthwhile to move `terminal_pack_content` into Lua. from `src/nvim/terminal.c`, you can call `nlua_call_vimfn` with a manually-constructed `typval_T`. [example](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/blob/03f746e913904ea8291d13ac7236f65a8c1eec26/src/nvim/help.c#L337-L342)
Lua can access this via `vim.api.nvim_get_chan_info(vim.o.channel)`
moving this to Lua also is worthwhile

Could we augment `:write` so that it handles terminal buffers? I.e. `:write` does what `:termsave` does, then we don't need `:termsave`.

And as a bonus, user can do `:write foo.mpack` if they want to save it somewhere else.

> why does it require a filename?

Yes, in my initial thought, nvim would 'assign' a name (which is a random id), but as you were saying, this name is unpredictable and not 'nvim-ish' either.

Since the path I choose here is to argument `:w` so that I think nvim would better save terminal buffers just like any other normal buffers, that is, specify a filename.

> Nvim should put the filename in a standard place (`stdpath('state')`, the same place where undo, swapfile, etc, are stored?)

If we consider saving it to `stdpath('state')/term/`, here would be too many implicit behaviors, including `:write` to somewhere not specified by users and giving this file a name users don't know. And I suspect users will get confused.

But I admit `stdpath('state')/term/` is a good path to store these files. Just can't think of a good, elegant way to do this. My previous solution is including saving to this path, but that one too is not clear/user-friendly enough.

> but it's weird to change behavior based on the file extension.

That's a fair concern. The only reason I used `.mpack` is to keep `:w foo.txt` in terminal buffers working as a plain text write. If that isn't acceptable, what about`:w ++term foo.mpack`?

> but i can't think of any vim feature that works like that.

perfectly true. consider `:w ++term foo.mpack`? I’m open to either. The `.mpack` approach is fewer keystrokes, but `++term` is more explicit.

comment_data.body:
doing this here is probably not the long-term solution, it seems hacky. 


- Only CMD_write/CMD_update are intercepted. :wq, :x, :wall, :saveas fall through to plain-text buf_write(). So `:w` saves state but `:wq` saves text?
- `:update` normally writes only if modified, but terminal buffers are never modified, so :update now always saves state (a semantic shift). Worth a deliberate decision + test.

anyway, it's usually better to start with a "userspace" approach, i.g. implement `BufWriteCmd` handler or something like that. because that's lower-risk, more flexible, and we always have the option in the future of going lower-level if we want.

also this bypasses `check_overwrite` and all BufWritePre/BufWritePost/BufWriteCmd autocmds.
E13/E17 are re-implemented in Lua, but that's kinda clumsy.
any user/plugin `autocmd BufWrite*` will silently no longer fire on a terminal `:w`. (probably very uncommon, but part of the puropse of this project is a more general idea to make terminals more useful and flexible for all kinds of purposes).

that's a good point, but more generally i am not convinced that plain text is something we need to support.

you can zoom out and ask: "what if we wanted to support even more formats?"
the answer isn't that we would build support for every random format, but rather we support one "base" format and make sure that the editor has tooling to convert it. but that's totally unrelated to terminal-specific features.

so the "base" format here is msgpack because terminals are binary data. making msgpack easy to work with is a complementary, but separate, project. 

and p.s., for plain text users still can copy-paste meanwhile?

It's `chan->stream.proc.cwd`. We can indeed expose it in Lua. But it is commonly recorded as "."
https://github.com/neovim/neovim/blob/c7707e2a10dc5551f7362f1dedd8c030f920b37d/src/nvim/eval/funcs.c#L3447-L3449
https://github.com/neovim/neovim/blob/c7707e2a10dc5551f7362f1dedd8c030f920b37d/src/nvim/eval/funcs.c#L3501

And Even if we expose this, it is still a spawn-time cwd and goes stale once `cd` is executed.
So for the future reference, I prefer the OSC 7 way. Maybe having `b:term_cwd` would be a good idea. WDYT?
